 Industry Professionals Dissect the Role of Laundry & Personal Care
 Society of Cosmetic Chemist Area I Chapters provide formulation tips and offer effective solutions for fabric and skin care product development. 
 November 16, 2026 
 By: Lianna Albrizio 
 Associate Editor , Happi 
 Save 
 From left: FemChem Beauty Founder Maria Plescia; Peter Tsolis, VP of research and development, skincare category, at the Estée Lauder Companies; and Valerie Gendelsman, senior manager, All, Laundry Detergent Product Development, Henkel. 
 Image caption -->
 The New York, Long Island, New England and Connecticut chapters of the Society of Cosmetic Chemists (SCC) welcomed formulators, marketers, cosmetic scientists, brand owners and others to Serafresca in Stamford, CT on Oct. 14 for a special educational event. 
 About three dozen attendees learned about formulation trends shaping the future of skin care and laundry products in this joint program the combined the Area I Chapters of SCC. The seminar, “What Touches Your Skin: The Role of Laundry and Personal Care Products,” was led by Peter Tsolis, VP of research and development, skincare category, at the Estée Lauder Companies. Speakers included Marisa Plescia, founder, FemChem Beauty and 2026 SCC president; Valerie Gendelsman, senior manager, All Laundry Detergent Products Development at Henkel; and Dr. Huifang Li, research fellow, University of Rhode Island; and keynote speaker Ellen Shepard, senior director, R&D Personal Care North America, Unilever .
 Similarities and Differences Between Laundry Detergents and Personal Care Products
 Gendelsman of Henkel lectured on the similarities and differences between laundry detergents and personal care products.
 Both laundry and personal care share the role of removing soil, wetting, foaming and emulsification. Surfactants in personal care are mild and produce a rich foam and creamy sensory feel while surfactants in laundry remove soil, clean grease and perform across wash conditions.
 “In personal care, there’s a lot more focus on mildness because you’re putting things directly onto skin,” said Gendelsman, adding that consumers seek a rich, creamy foam if handwashing or shampooing to signify functionality.
 Another similar function is fragrances, dyes and aesthetics with a shared role of communicating performance through senses with different priorities. Personal care focuses on luxury experience, personal identity and variant-specific cues. Laundry focuses on cleanliness signal, long-lasting freshness and differentiation.
 “With laundry, it’s more of a commodity in general,” she said. “You’re not focused on as much luxury or personalization. In laundry, a lot of the fragrance, dyes and aesthetics decisions, they are trying to communicate that your product is cleaning and so a lot of fragrance types are all in a similar category because you do primarily have to communicate to the consumer that your clothes are clean.”
 She said long-lasting freshness claims exist more in the laundry category given the need for fresh-smelling clothes for days or preventing garments from getting musty odors. Laundry and personal are also share the similar function of stability and processing aids. Specifically, viscosity/pH control, phase stability, solubilization and preservation. In Personal Care, this includes differentiation through rheology; “free from” claims; and premium. Laundry involves phase separation, dual-benefit ingredients and salt-sensitive.
 Performance enhancers are another similar function. Requirements diverge because of substrate. Biological factors like hair and skin, include biological barrier, mild chemistry and balance cleaning and care. Fabrics involve cotton and polyester; are inert; no biological barrier function; tolerates aggressive chemistry; and maximum soil removal.
 “For personal care, you’re trying to balance the cleaning and the care, whereas with fabrics, you’re trying to maximize your soil removal,” she noted.
 Enzymes are another performance enhancer. They are specific to stain types, like lock and key. When the correct stain binds to the active site, chemical reactions occur to break down the stain into smaller pieces. Protease degrades protein-based soils (blood, grass, egg, milk); amylase degrades starch-based soils (sauce, gravy); mannanase degrades gum-based soils (ice cream, sauce, dressing); and cellulase removes damaged/frayed fibers (cotton).
 Detergents work to remove soils; prevent redeposition; control foam; work in hard water; and function across temperatures. Examples include enzymes, anti-redepositon polymers and chelants. Chelants binds ions in metal-containing stains (red wine, blood, grass, tea). Colorimetry can be used to see how well a detergent fights stains by measuring the stain’s color change after wash tests using surfactant-based stains, bleachable stains and enzymatic stains.
 The Evolution of Our Relationship with Skin
 Tsolis of Estée Lauder discussed skin aging and how using the right products and dosage can keep the skin’s microbiome youthful for as long as possible. Collagen, the structural protein responsible for skin’s firmness, reduces as people age, with a more profound effect on women’s skin, given men’s denser composition.
 “It’s hard to make a universal product for everybody, but these are the things we think about when we make our products,” he said.
 Sun exposure, seasonality, lifestyle choices and the body’s natural aging process, he said, all factor into skin health. For example, post-menopausal women see a 30% collagen reduction in the first five years, which can have an adverse effect on elasticity.
 “It’s a moving target when you think about skin and what we need,” he said. “It’s a constant shift looking at consumers and what they feel is going on with their skin and responding to the ever-changing needs they have.”
 In midlife, 10% of sebaceous glands are going to start dropping, triggering acne and dryness, triggering a hormonal shift like re-experiencing puberty. Despite similar changes, there is a drastic difference in purchasing habits between these generations with respect to leveraging their knowledge about health and wellness.
 Moreover, new technology and novel ingredient trends are shaping formulation and addressing these ever-changing dynamics.
Given sensitivity’s common complaint, Tsolis highlighted Clinique’s Daily Calm . The skincare and makeup collection was created for a variety of skin issues. The products— which range from a makeup-foundation balm to a gentle cream cleanser—are clinically proven to instantly soothe, help repair and prevent future irritation.
 Tsolis said these “multi-franchises” are necessary to address all concerns; however, more doesn’t necessarily equate to better. He said higher concentration does not automatically produce a better product experience; higher levels of retinoids or acids can increase dryness and irritation; an ingredient percentage does not account for the base or the delivery approach. For sensitive skin, optimization may matter more than maximization.
 In terms of language, pro-aging is preferred over “anti-aging” rooted in a more realistic over idealistic view. For example, “clear” is evolving to “calm,” “bright” to “radiant,” “smooth” to “comfortable” and “wrinkle-free” to “resilient.”
 Moreover, when it comes to formulation direction, he preached prevention over rescue, personalized support for fluctuating needs and barrier-first efficacy with “fewer, smarter” products.
 “There’s going to be those traditional, iconic products that we’re all going to have to develop and are the heroes behind our brands but looking at alternative forms with different visible deliveries are really going to evolve around the future for consumers to feel the connection of efficacy and the habitat the active is going to live in,” said Tsolis.
 Clinique’s Daily Calm are clinically proven to instantly soothe, help repair and prevent future irritation . 
 He said evolving ingredient technology is factoring in therapeutic experience over mere mechanical or those apply to the five senses. These include micro needles, or natural silica spicules called beauty spicules which open physical pathways through the stratum corneum for active delivery; carbonated formats which create visible bubbling during application; lipophilic microcapsules in clear systems to indicate delivery vesicle (claims about skin penetration or increased circulation require product specific evidence, Tsolis noted); and cryo-skincare, a sub-zero ice delivery formulation which is frozen before use and turns intense heat skincare into a chilled sensory ritual creating a crisp, sorbet-like cooling on contact.
 AI will also play a role in the formulation’s future, added Tsolis.
 “Designing a product with AI capabilities or designing an ingredient with technology is one aspect. Designing them in tandem to the relationship with someone’s skin is going to be the unlock,” he said.
 Future skincare products, he added, must work with procedures and support recovery, extend results and protect the barrier. Topical alternatives include peptide-rich formulations which offer needle-less wrinkle reduction, weaker muscle contraction and faster relaxation. He added Asian markets already treat post-procedure recovery as its own shelf, alongside other targeted skincare categories. Acoustic penetration of actives and device-assisted delivery will move clinical mechanisms into the consumer’s home.
 Functionality of ingredients, particularly in the world of simplification, is a key trend that is going to amplify with consumers. The Innovation Triangle provides “balance” over “trade-off.” This entails bioactive (potency and mechanism of action); delivery (route and release); and texture (rheology and sensory).
 Bioactives drive efficacy on skin and clinical performance. They communicate with skin on a cellular level, and trigger changes regeneration, barrier repair brightening calming. The delivery system decides whether an active survives the formula and partitions into skin and reaches its target. Texture governs contact time and film behavior on skin, serum, lotion, cream are the consumer’s first read on whether the product is working. He also noted the importance of the delivery system.
 “You look at molecular weight; you look at polarity; you look at where in the skin you want to target these types of actives. It’s a huge, very technical endeavor we go after, but the most exciting thing we work on. We know if we get it right, the consumer testing is visible and can be quicker and more adaptive to consumer needs.”
 Tsolis said bioactives have several barriers to overcome including solubility; penetration; active integrity; and release delivery to the MOA site. He recommends a better active performance without relying on a higher dose – and with less irritation than concentration-led approaches.
 How SPF Formulation Influences Your Skin Beyond UV Protection
 Plescia of FemChem Beauty and SCC lectured on the imperativeness of daily sunscreen use and the factors responsible for optimal functioning and sun protection.
 “Sunscreen is evolving from a beach-day necessity into an essential step in daily skincare routines,” said Plescia.
 Increased awareness of photography, hyperpigmentation and skin cancer is encouraging consumers to prioritize daily photo protection. Skincare education, dermatologists and beauty influencers are helping normalize year-round SPF use , particularly among younger consumers. Beauty enthusiasts expect lightweight textures, invisible finishes and compatibility with makeup. Consequently, sunscreens are evolving into multifunctional skincare products, combining UV protection with the sensory and functional benefits of moisturizers, serums and primers.
 According to the latest data from American Academy of Dermatology, 96% of Americans believe that sun protection is important; 57% report using sunscreen daily; and 20% report wearing sunscreen on cloudy days.
 “Sunscreen is no longer simply viewed as protection from the sun; it’s increasingly becoming the foundation of preventative daily skincare routines,” noted Plescia.
 Organic or “hemical” filters absorb the UV radiation and emits the energy as often fluorescence or phosphoresce, transferring to another molecule, or negligible heat (triplet state), examples are the octocrylene, homosalate and the newly US FDA-approved BEMT .
 Inorganic UV filters or “mineral” filters include zinc oxide and titanium dioxide and absorb, reflect and refract. Both are semiconductor materials/crystalline structure that allow light to be absorbed through the photelectric effect.
 “A UV filter system alone does not equal sunscreen performance,” said Plescia. “Within that sunscreen itself there is also the solubility, stability, the spreading, the film distribution the dry-down —all those plus many more interact to become an effective delivered photoprotection system.”
 In terms of ingredient synergy, skin soothing and antioxidant ingredients help reduce UV-induced erythema and further protect the skin from UV-induced damage. Iron oxides can help “tint” the sunscreen to mitigate whitening and may provide some additional UV protection. Powders can fill in the “gaps” in the sunscreen film and aesthetic modifiers.
 Combination/hybrid UV filters have synergistic benefits including UVA/UVB absorption and UV filters in both the external and internal phase. Research by Sohn et al. (2014) in the paper, “Film thickness frequency distribution of different vehicles determines sunscreen efficacy,” demonstrates that sunscreen vehicle composition and application conditions significantly influence film thickness distribution and measured SPF. The vehicle is the viscosity and oil-phase structure; film formation is the thickness and distribution on skin; and SPF efficacy is measured UV protection.
 “The formulation vehicle is not simply a carrier for UV filters,” she said. “It’s physical properties help determine how effectively the sunscreen forms a protective layer on the skin.”
 Environmental stress impacts sunscreen film. Heat and evaporation accelerate volatile loss, may alter film thickness, UV filter solubility and distribution. Solvents, emollients, polymers and film formers influence residual film structure. Movement causes potential cracking, displacement or loss of film uniformity, depending on film flexibility. Formulation considerations include flexible film formers, plasticizing emollient and skin adhesion. Water can affect film adhesion, continuity and retention on the skin. Formulation considerations include film-forming polymers, emulsifiers and emollients influence water resistance and substantivity.
 Friction causes mechanical disruption, uneven coverage and transfer from the skin. Formulation considerations include film flexibility, cohesion, adhesion, and mechanical durability influence wear resistance.
 “The skin will also have an effect on sunscreen and how it sits on our skin: lipids, hydration, sebum and microenvironment on our skin – all of that is going to effective potentially photoprotection, photo stability the film integrity and water resistance, our hydration and our skin comfort and tolerability,” she said.
 Research by Keshavarzi et al. (2022) in the paper “Enhancing the Sweat Resistance of Sunscreens” investigated how film-forming polymers and water-absorbing particles influence sunscreen retention. UV-filter distribution, and SPF during perspiration. Sweat can reduce protection through both sunscreen wash-off (loss of film thickness) and redistribution (loss of film uniformity).
 According to the paper: Film formers improve substantivity. Hydrophobic film-forming polymers reduced wash-off, but higher concentration did not necessarily provide better SPF retention.
 Film uniformity is critical: A formulation with 0.75% film former retained higher in vitro SPF after sweating than one containing 3% despite the higher concentration reducing wash-off more effectively.
 Particle properties matter. Small water-absorbing particles capable of forming gel-like structures reduced wash-off and redistribution, while larger swelling particles could disrupt UV-filter distribution.
 Regarding Skin Typography, Gebauer et al. (2012) in the paper “Influence of Skin Aging Effects on the Skin Surface Profile and Sunscreen Distribution,” researched how skin surface topography, furrow volume and age-related changes in skin elasticity influence the uniformity of sunscreen distribution on human skin.
 Skin topography influences sunscreen deposition. Natural skin furrows and surface irregularities affect how sunscreen spreads and distributes across the skin. Film uniformity correlates with skin furrow volume: the researchers identified a clear correlation between measured skin furrow volume and spectroscopically determined sunscreen film inhomogeneity.
 Skin elasticity plays a role. Age-related reduction in skin elasticity was associated with more homogenous sunscreen distribution in individual measurements.
 Chronological age was a significant predictor. Despite individual differences, average sunscreen distribution characteristics were not statistically different between younger (under 32) and older (51 years and above) participants.
